sections.text: Efficiency of bone marrow-derived cells in the treatment of experimental autoimmune type 1 diabetes: immunomodulatory and anti-apoptotic properties
Background

Bone marrow-derived cell (BMDC) transplantation is increasingly recognized as a valuable strategy in regenerative therapies. However, the data regarding the impact of BMDC transplantation on the severity of diabetes mellitus type 1 (DMT1).
Aim
This study aimed to determine the effectiveness of adoptive transfer of BMDC isolated from either non-diabetic mice (nBMDC) or diabetic mice (dBMDC) in the treatment of a DMT1 mouse model.
Methods

Male Swiss albino mice underwent a 16-hour fasting period, followed by administration of streptozotocin (STZ) at a dose of 40 mg/kg body weight for five days to induce DMT1. After 14 days, diabetic mice were divided into four groups. The first group served as a diabetic control and received sodium citrate buffer, while the remaining three groups were treated for two weeks with one of the following: subcutaneous (s.c.) administration of insulin (8 U/kg/day), intravenous (i.v.) inoculation of nBMDCs (1 × 106 cells/mouse/once), or i.v. injections of dBMDC (1 × 106 cells/mouse/once).
Results

STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with either nBMDC or dBMDC exhibited a noticeable increase in the expression of CD4+ T lymphocytes, CD8+ T lymphocytes, and NK lymphocytes, myeloid granulocytic neutrophil (CD11b+/Ly-6G+ cells), monocytic macrophage (CD11b+/Ly-6G− cells), and monocytic CD11b+/Ly-6G− cells. Additionally, there was a marked reduction in the percentages of CD25+ T cells, Foxp3+ cells, regulatory T cells (Tregs), CD25+/Foxp3+ cells, Treg CD25+/Foxp3− cells, Treg CD4+/CD25+ cells, and Treg CD4+/CD25− cells within the myeloid cell population in the spleen. The therapeutic efficacy of BMDC as an anti-diabetic therapy was further supported by a significant reduction in the proportion of early and late apoptosis in splenic leukocytes, accompanied by a slight increase in necrosis in STZ-induced DMT1 mice receiving either nBMDC or dBMDC.
Conclusion

In summary, adoptive transfer of BMDCs exerts significant immunomodulatory and anti-apoptotic effects on pancreatic β cells, which are beneficial for pancreatic islets in DMT1 mice. Clinical studies are warranted to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of the adoptive transfer of BMDCs as a potential therapy for autoimmune DMT1.
Introduction

Diabetes Mellitus Type 1 (DMT1) is characterized by the destruction of insulin-secreting β-cells in the pancreas, resulting in a complete deficiency of insulin production. The DMT1 condition is primarily driven by an autoimmune mechanism, in which autoreactive T cells target and damage pancreatic β-cells, causing insulitis and the subsequent loss of islet β-cells. The resulting lack of insulin production leads to hyperglycemia and disrupts the metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids. While evidence suggests that both environmental influences and genetic susceptibility contribute to the risk of developing immune disorders in DMT1 patients, the precise etiology of immune system dysfunction in this condition remains unclear.

Currently, treatment and preventive options for DMT1 are limited, primarily relying on lifelong insulin replacement therapy to regulate blood glucose levels. However, insulin therapy only supplements the body’s insulin deficiency and cannot fully restore pancreatic function or regenerate β-cells. Management of TDM1 typically involves insulin injections and dietary control, but these methods cannot mimic the body’s natural ability to produce insulin, which may result in potentially life-threatening complications like severe hyperglycemic attacks or hypoglycemic shocks. In some cases, insulin therapy alone may be insufficient to control the progression of diabetes and its associated complications, making alternative therapeutic approaches more desirable. One such alternative is the transplantation of pancreatic islet cells or the entire pancreas. However, this method is limited by scarcity and the risk of immune rejection. Therefore, the most promising therapeutic strategy involves stimulating the regeneration of the body’s own endogenous β-cells. Research has increasingly focused on stem cell therapy as a potential treatment for DMT1.

Bone marrow-derived stem cells (BMDSC) have the potential to address DMT1 through their immunomodulatory characteristics and their ability to differentiate into insulin-secreting cells. This is important because DMT1 is an autoimmune disorder in which immune cells attack and destroy pancreatic β-cells. BMDSC therapy can help regulate blood glucose levels and reduce significant fluctuations; however, it cannot completely prevent the development of complications, including microvascular, macrovascular, and neuropathic issues. Therefore, generating new β-cells remains a critical component of DMT1 treatment.

There are two primary categories of BMDSC: hematopoietic stem cells (BM-HSC) and mesenchymal stem cells (BM-MSC). Both types can promote the regeneration of β-cells. BM-HSCs give rise to all myeloid and lymphoid cell lineages, including endothelial precursor cells, which play a crucial role in promoting microvascular angiogenesis. The pancreatic vascular endothelium significantly influences β-cell regeneration by stimulating β-cell differentiation from progenitor cells. Additionally, it provides essential signals, such as hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), which support β-cell proliferation and enhance their functionality.

BM-MSC transplantation is administered peripherally; it activates various mechanisms and improves islet cell function in patients with DMT1. These mechanisms include the release of growth factors (GFs) and cytokines, the promotion of vascularization and angiogenesis, and the regeneration of endogenous stem cells. These processes contribute to the repair and vascularization of under-perfused areas and the modulation of inflammatory and fibrosis processes. In the case of DMT1, BM-HSC transplantation improves islet cell function by eliminating autoreactive T cells and creating a less inflammatory environment. The use of BM-MSC therapy utilizing for DMT1 demonstrates efficacy due to its strong immunoregulatory capacity.

BM-MSC exhibit a significant capacity to differentiate into β-cell-like organoids, thereby increasing the islet mass. Furthermore, they demonstrate immunomodulatory properties by suppressing the immune response of T helper type 1 (Th1) cells and T cells through inflammatory pathways and transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β). These characteristics are particularly relevant in the context of DMT1. Given the ability of stem cells to differentiate into insulin-producing cells and their potential to restore immune tolerance, stem cell therapy shows promise as a treatment option for DMT1. The application of BM-MSCs and human umbilical cord stem cell (HUCSCs)-derived exosomes has demonstrated beneficial effects on insulin levels, hyperglycemia, and insulin responsiveness. Therapies involving. BM-MSCs and HUCMSCs in DMT1 have also shown potential in reversing autoimmunity and improving blood glucose control.

In the field of regenerative medicine focused on treating diabetes, bone marrow-derived cells (BMDC) are considered a promising option for generating pancreatic β-cells. There is ongoing debate about whether these BMDC can transform into β-cells or if they primarily promote β-cell formation indirectly. Research has demonstrated that BMDC can indeed differentiate directly into β-cells. Furthermore, bone marrow transplantation (BMT) has been shown to reduce elevated blood glucose levels (hyperglycemia) in diabetic animals and support β-cells regeneration following damage caused by streptozotocin (STZ). The infiltration of bone marrow-derived cells (BMC) near the islets in STZ-DMT1 mice undergoing BMT suggests that these cells may play a role in activating the proliferation and transformation of stem or progenitor cells into β-cells.

The management of DMT1 not only maintains stable blood glucose levels but also addresses immune system imbalances. BMC exhibits properties that can modulate the immune response through multiple pathways. They interact with CD4+ T and CD8+ T cells via the programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) molecule, release nitric oxide (NO), and regulate lymphocyte proliferation by inhibiting mitogen activity. These characteristics suggest that BMC can restrict the development of T cells, including those targeting glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD). Transplantation of BMDC has shown promising outcomes in modulating the immune response, reducing inflammation, and enhancing T-cell regulation. BMDC transplantation significantly influences the immune system by restoring the equilibrium between type 1 and type 2 helper T cells (Th1 and Th2), modulating cytokine levels, and supporting local immune regulation, thereby protecting pancreatic β cells from lymphocyte-mediated damage. Additionally, BMT may enhance the secretion of chemokines, which subsequently affects the functions of T cells, antigen-presenting cells, and lymphocytes. This modulation could potentially reverse autoantibody production and contribute to the comprehensive management of diabetes.

The purpose of this research is to evaluate the immune system-modulating and cell anti-apoptotic potentials of adoptive transfer of BMDCs isolated from either non-diabetic mice (nBMDCs) or diabetic mice (dBMDCs). Additionally, the study will investigate the efficacy of adoptive transfer of BMDC in treating DMT1 in STZ-induced DMT1 mice.
Materials and methods
Antibodies and reagents

Streptozotocin (STZ) (Sigma-Aldrich, UK), used for diabetes induction in mice, was aliquoted in 0.1 M sodium-citrate buffer. RPMI-1640 medium (Invitrogen, California, USA) enriched with 5% fetal calf serum (FCS) (Invitrogen), an antibiotic mixture (penicillin 100 µg/ml and streptomycin 100 µg/ml), non-essential amino acids (NEAA), 2 mM L-glutamine, and 1 mM sodium pyruvate. 10× RBC lysis buffer (Invitrogen, California, USA). Anti-mouse CD4 monoclonal antibody (Clone#: GK1.5), anti-mouse CD8 monoclonal antibody (Clone#: YTS169.4), anti-mouse CD133 monoclonal antibody (Clone#: 29A1.4), anti-mouse CD11b monoclonal antibody (Clone#: 5C6), anti-mouse Ly-6G monoclonal antibody (Clone#: 1A8), anti-mouse CD25 monoclonal antibody (Clone#: PC61.5.3) (Bio-Rad, California, USA), anti-mouse FOXP3 monoclonal antibody (Clone#: FJK-16s) (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, California, USA), and Annexin V and PI (eBioscience, San Diego, USA) were used.
Mice

Fifty male Swiss albino mice, aged 6 to 8 weeks and weighing approximately 25 ± 2 g, were delivered from the National Research Centre (Giza, Egypt). The mice were distributed into five groups, each consisting of ten animals. The study strictly adhered to the ARRIVE guidelines to ensure optimal care throughout all procedures. Additionally, all procedures were conducted ethically and with compassion. Euthanasia was performed by the inhalation of carbon dioxide (CO2) followed by cervical dislocation. The procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the Science Faculty, Tanta University, Egypt (ethical approval code: IACUC-SCI-TU-00487), ensuring proper care, accommodation, and methods to minimize suffering and distress among the animals.
Induction of Diabetes Mellitus Type 1(DMT1)

Diabetes mellitus type 1 (DMT1) was induced in experimental mice by administering streptozotocin (STZ) at a dose of 40 mg/kg body weight. STZ was dissolved in 0.1 M sodium citrate buffer and delivered via multiple intraperitoneal (i.p.) injections over a continuous five days. To prevent hypoglycemia resulting from STZ administration, the mice were provided with a 10% (w/v) glucose. Control mice received an equivalent volume of sodium citrate buffer as a vehicle. After completing the dosing regimen, the STZ-treated mice were maintained under standard conditions for nine days. At the end of this period, the mice exhibited signs of diabetes, confirmed by fasting blood glucose levels ≥ 250 mg/dL. To assess blood glucose, the STZ-treated mice were fasted for 12 h, and blood samples were collected from the tail vein. Mice with fasting blood glucose levels ≥ 250 mg/dL were classified as diabetic and selected for further studies.
Preparation of Bone Marrow-Derived Cells (BMDCs)

Unfractionated bone marrow-derived cells (BMDC) were obtained from either non-diabetic mice (nBMDC) or diabetic mice (dBMDC) as follows: the tibiae and femurs were dissected from the mice, and the medullary cavities were flushed with 5 ml of PBS containing 2% FBS. A single-cell suspension was generated by mechanical dissociation, achieved by sequentially passing the cells through needles of progressively smaller gauges. The freshly collected (nBMDC) and (dBMDC) were washed two times and aliquoted in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Subsequently, the cells were treated with 10× RBC lysis buffer and rinsed two additional times before being suspended in RPMI 1640 enriched with 5% FCS. This suspension was then centrifuged at 400 g for 5 min at 20 °C and subsequently resuspended in 1 ml of RPMI-1640 medium. Finally, nBMDC and dBMDC (1 × 106 cells/mouse) were transferred into STZ-induced DMT1 mice through the mice’s lateral tail veins.
Experimental design

STZ-diabetic mice were randomly grouped into 4 groups, each consisting of ten mice. On the 15th day after DMT1 induction, the first group (STZ group) received an intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of citrate buffer. The second group (STZ/Insulin group) was administered insulin (8 U/kg/day) via a subcutaneous (s.c.) injection. The third group (STZ/nBMDCs group) received a single intravenous (i.v.) injection of BMDC from non-diabetic (naïve) mice (nBMDC) at a dose of 1 × 106 cells/mouse. The fourth group (STZ/dBMDCs group) was given a one-time i.v. injection of BMDC from STZ-diabetic mice (dBMDC) at a dose of 1 × 106 cells/mouse. Additionally, a naïve control group (naïve group) was administered sodium citrate buffer via i.p. injection. On the 28th day following STZ injection, all mice were euthanized, and their serum and spleens were gathered for further investigations.
Flow cytometry

A total of 1 × 106 splenocytes collected from experimental mice were labeled with anti-mouse CD4, CD8, CD133, CD11b, Ly-6G, CD25, and FOXP3 antibody. The antibody-labeled splenocytes were then incubated in the dark at room temperature for 30 min, followed by cooling on ice for 1 min. After two washing cycles, the cells were resuspended in 0.3 ml of a solution containing 0.5% bovine serum albumin and 0.02% sodium azide. Flow cytometry analysis was performed using a FACS Calibur system (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA), and data analysis was conducted using Cell-Quest (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA).
Flowcytometric analysis of apoptosis

The splenocyte single-cell suspension was washed with cold PBS, resuspended in 10X annexin-binding buffer at 1 × 106 cells/ml, placed into 1.5-ml Eppendorf tubes, then stained with 5 µL of annexin V-fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC), along with 1 µL of PI working solution (100 µg/ml). The stained cells were incubated at room temperature for 15 min, followed by the addition of 400 µL of 1X annexin-binding buffer, careful mixing, and keeping on ice. Subsequently, splenocytes were examined using flow cytometry.
Statistical analysis

The results are presented as mean ± standard error (SE) (n = 10 mice/group). A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed, followed by post hoc tests, including Tukey’s HSD and Dunnett’s test. A P-value less than 0.05 was deemed statistically significant.
Results
Potential of adoptive transfer of BMDCs on the expression of lymphocytes and myeloid cells

Phenotypic analysis of splenic CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and myeloid cells from STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with either nBMDC or dBMDC was performed using flow cytometry. Immunophenotyping results revealed that the relative percentage of CD4+ T cells was significantly elevated in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with citrate buffer, insulin, nBMDC, or dBMDC compared to naïve non-diabetic mice receiving citrate buffer (Fig. 1A). Conversely, our data showed a reduction in CD4+ T cell expression in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with insulin, nBMDC, or dBMDC compared to those receiving citrate buffer (Fig. 1A). Furthermore, treatment with nBMDC or dBMDC resulted in a notable decrease in CD4+ T cells relative to insulin-treated STZ-induced DMT1 mice (Fig. 1A). Specifically, phenotypic expression of CD4+ T cells was significantly lower in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with insulin, nBMDC, or dBMDC compared to those treated with citrate, buffer (42.55 ± 1.00%, 22.73 ± 0.78%, and 29.10 ± 0.72%, respectively, versus 47.87 ± 2.30%) (Fig. 1B).

A remarkable elevation in the proportion of CD4+ T cells in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with citrate buffer, insulin, nBMDCs, or dBMDCs compared to naïve non-diabetic mice (47.87 ± 2.30%, 42.55 ± 1.00%, 22.73 ± 0.78%, and 29.10 ± 0.72%, respectively, versus 12.73 ± 0.60%) (Fig. 1B). Furthermore, treatment of STZ-induced DMT1 mice with nBMDCs or dBMDCs resulted in a reduction of CD4+ T cell levels relative to receiving insulin (22.73 ± 0.78% and 29.10 ± 0.72%, respectively, versus 42.55 ± 1.00%) (Fig. 1B).

Findings showed that CD8+ T cell expression was lower in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with insulin, nBMDC, or dBMDC compared to STZ-induced T1DM mice receiving a citrate buffer. In contrast, splenic CD8+ T cell expression was notably higher in STZ-induced DMT1 mice receiving sodium citrate, insulin, nBMDCs, or dBMDCs relative to naïve mice treated with citrate buffer. Furthermore, inoculation with nBMDCs or dBMDCs in STZ-induced DMT1 mice resulted in a significant decrease in CD8+ T cells compared to those treated with insulin (Fig. 2A). Specifically, the phenotypic expression of CD8+ T cells in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with insulin, nBMDCs, or dBMDCs was significantly lower than in those receiving citrate buffer (42.28 ± 1.68%, 21.28 ± 0.96%, and 30.85 ± 1.56%, respectively, versus 56.47 ± 1.23%) (Fig. 2B). The expression of CD8+ T cells in STZ-induced DMT1 mice receiving sodium citrate, insulin, nBMDCs, or dBMDCs was significantly higher compared to naïve non-diabetic mice receiving a buffer of sodium citrate (56.47 ± 1.23%, 42.28 ± 1.68%, 21.28 ± 0.96%, and 30.85 ± 1.56%, respectively, versus 15.57 ± 0.44%) (Fig. 2B). Administration of nBMDCs or dBMDCs in STZ-induced DMT1 mice led to a notable decrease in CD8 + T cells compared to those treated with insulin (21.28 ± 0.96% and 30.85 ± 1.56%, respectively, versus 42.28 ± 1.68%) (Fig. 2B).

The findings presented herein revealed that the expression of CD25+T cells was higher in STZ-induced DMT1 mice receiving insulin, nBMDC, or dBMDC compared to naïve non-diabetic mice. Conversely, the proportion of CD25+ T cell expression was lower in STZ-induced DMT1 mice receiving insulin, nBMDCs, or dBMDCs compared to those administered citrate buffer. Furthermore, treatment with nBMDC or dBMDC in STZ-induced DMT1 mice resulted in an obvious decrease in CD25+T cells compared to the group of STZ-induced DMT1 mice administered insulin (Fig. 3A). A substantial increase in the phenotypic expression of CD25+ T cells in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with citrate buffer, insulin, nBMDC, or dBMDC compared to naïve non-diabetic mice (29.45 ± 0.67%, 21.78 ± 0.40%, 10.90 ± 0.48%, and 13.53 ± 1.10%, respectively, versus 29.7%) (Fig. 3B). There was a remarkable decrease in the phenotype expression rate of CD25+ T cells in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with insulin, nBMDC, or dBMDC compared to those receiving citrate buffer (21.78 ± 0.40%, 10.90 ± 0.48%, and 13.53 ± 1.10%, respectively, versus 29.45 ± 0.67%) (Fig. 3B). Treatment of STZ-induced DMT1 mice with nBMDC or dBMDC caused a significant decrease in CD25+ T cells compared to those receiving insulin (10.90 ± 0.48% and 13.53 ± 1.10%, respectively, versus 21.78 ± 0.40%) (Fig. 3B).

Furthermore, the relative percentage of NKp46+ cell expression was notably elevated in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with insulin, nBMDC, or dBMDC compared to naïve non-diabetic mice. Conversely, the relative percentage of NKp46+ cell expression was significantly reduced in STZ-induced DMT1 mice receiving insulin, nBMDCs, or dBMDCs compared to those administered citrate buffer. Additionally, treatment of STZ-induced DMT1 mice with nBMDCs resulted in a substantial reduction in splenic NKp46+ cells relative to those treated with insulin (Fig. 4A). These findings demonstrate that the phenotypic expression of splenic NKp46+ cells was significantly increased in STZ-induced DMT1 mice receiving citrate buffer, insulin, nBMDC, or dBMDC compared to naïve mice receiving citrate buffer (55.60 ± 1.25%, 43.25 ± 0.53%, 25.30 ± 1.28%, and 39.45 ± 1.33%, respectively, versus 19.8 ± 1.35%) (Fig. 4B). The data presented indicate that the relative rate of phenotypic expression of NKp46+ cells was significantly lower in STZ-induced DMT1 mice that received insulin, nBMDCs, or dBMDCs, compared to those receiving a buffer of sodium citrate (43.25 ± 0.53%, 25.30 ± 1.28%, and 39.45 ± 1.33%, respectively, versus 55.60 ± 1.25%) (Fig. 4B). Administration of nBMDCs to STZ-induced DMT1 mice caused a significant decrease in NKp46+ cells compared to those receiving insulin (25.30 ± 1.28% versus 43.25 ± 0.53%) (Fig. 4B).

Analysis revealed an increase in the relative percentage of splenic Foxp3+ cells in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with citrate buffer, insulin, or nBMDC compared to naïve non-diabetic mice. However, the data also showed a reduction in the relative expression of splenic Foxp3+ cells in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with insulin, nBMDC, or dBMDC compared to those receiving citrate buffer. Notably, adoptive transfer of nBMDC or dBMDC in STZ-induced DMT1 mice resulted in a decrease in Foxp3+ cells relative to those treated with insulin (Fig. 5A). Specifically, the phenotypic expression of splenic Foxp3+ cells was significantly elevated in STZ-induced DMT1 mice receiving citrate buffer, insulin, or nBMDCs compared to naïve non-diabetic mice (46.75 ± 1.93%, 31.98 ± 1.82%, 17.03 ± 0.40%, respectively, versus 13.02 ± 0.97%) (Fig. 5B). Additionally, the data revealed a decrease in the relative rate of phenotypic expression of splenic Foxp3+ cells in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with insulin, nBMDCs, or dBMDCs compared to those receiving citrate buffer (31.98 ± 1.82%, 17.03 ± 0.40%, and 10.83 ± 0.28%, respectively, versus 10.83 ± 0.28%) (Fig. 5B). Administration of nBMDC or dBMDC to STZ-induced DMT1 mice caused a significant reduction in Foxp3+ cells compared to insulin-treated mice (17.03 ± 0.40% and 10.83 ± 0.28%, respectively, versus 21.78 ± 0.40%) (Fig. 5B).

The study indicates that the inoculation of nBMDCs or dBMDCs significantly reduced the elevated expression of splenic myeloid cells in diabetic mice. Specifically, the phenotypic expression of myeloid CD11b+/Ly-6G+ cells was increased in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with citrate buffer, insulin, nBMDC, or dBMDC relative to naïve non-diabetic mice. In contrast, treating STZ-induced DMT1 mice with insulin, along with nBMDC or dBMDC, led to a notable decrease in myeloid granulocytic neutrophil cells (CD11b+/Ly-6G+) when compared to STZ-induced DMT1 mice receiving citrate buffer. Furthermore, treatment of STZ-induced DMT1 mice with nBMDC or dBMDC resulted in a lower relative percentage of CD11b+/Ly-6G+ cells compared to those treated with insulin (Fig. 6A). However, the phenotypic expression of myeloid CD11b+/Ly-6G− cells was significantly reduced in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with citrate buffer, insulin, nBMDC, or dBMDC compared to naïve non-diabetic mice. Additionally, the injection of insulin or nBMDC into STZ-induced DMT1 mice decreased the population of myeloid monocytic macrophage CD11b+/Ly-6G− cells compared to those receiving citrate buffer. Moreover, treatment with nBMDC or dBMDC further reduced the relative percentage of CD11b+/Ly-6G− cells compared to insulin treatment alone (Fig. 6A).

The findings revealed a marked increase in the phenotypic expression of myeloid CD11b+/Ly-6G+ cells in STZ-induced DMT1 mice receiving citrate buffer, insulin, nBMDCs, or dBMDCs, compared to naïve non-diabetic mice (51.23 ± 2.40%, 36.98 ± 3.67%, 18.38 ± 0.60%, and 22.75 ± 0.80%, respectively, versus 13.0%) (Fig. 6B1). Furthermore, the administration of insulin, nBMDC, or dBMDC to STZ-induced DMT1 mice induced a significant reduction in myeloid granulocytic neutrophil cells (CD11b+/Ly-6G+) compared to STZ-induced DMT1 mice that received a citrate buffer (36.98 ± 3.67%, 18.38 ± 0.60%, and 22.75 ± 0.80%, respectively, versus 51.23 ± 2.40%) (Fig. 6B1). Additionally, treatment of STZ-induced DMT1 mice with nBMDC or dBMDC resulted in a notable decrease in the relative percentage of CD11b+/Ly-6G+ cells compared to those treated with insulin (18.38 ± 0.60% and 22.75 ± 0.80%, respectively, versus 36.98 ± 3.67%) (Fig. 6B1).

The expression of myeloid CD11b+/Ly-6G− cells was significantly lower in STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with citrate buffer, insulin, nBMDC, or dBMDC compared to naïve non-diabetic mice (5.50 ± 0.18%, 7.96 ± 0.08%, 6.58 ± 0.09%, and 4.43 ± 0.20% versus 9.28 ± 0.32%, respectively) (Fig. 6B2). Treatment of STZ-induced DMT1 mice with insulin or nBMDCs resulted in a notable decrease in the population of myeloid monocytic macrophage cells (CD11b+/Ly-6G−) compared to STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with citrate buffer (7.96 ± 0.08% and 6.58 ± 0.09% versus 5.50 ± 0.18%, respectively) (Fig. 6B2). Furthermore, administration of nBMDCs or dBMDCs to STZ-induced DMT1 mice caused a remarkable reduction in the relative percentage of CD11b+/Ly-6G− cells compared to those treated with insulin (6.58 ± 0.09% and 4.43 ± 0.20% versus 7.96 ± 0.08%, respectively) (Fig. 6B2).
Potential of adoptive transfer of BMDCs on the expression of regulatory T lymphocytes

STZ-induced DMT1 mice treated with citrate buffer, insulin, or nBMDC exhibited a significant decrease in the expression of Treg (CD25+/Foxp3+) compared to naïve non-diabetic mice. Conversely, treating STZ-induced DMT1 mice with insulin, along with nBMDC or dBMDC, resulted in a remarkable reduction in the relative percentage of CD25+/Foxp3+ cells compared to those administered a citrate buffer. Discussion

DMT1 represents a significant health challenge in the 21st century, with an increasing incidence observed worldwide. Although cell therapy is a crucial method for replacing damaged β-cells, the presence of autoantibodies diminishes its efficacy over time, resulting in the reemergence of diabetes mellitus. Therefore, there is an urgent need for a therapeutic strategy that can restore insulin-producing cells while inhibiting autoimmune damage simultaneously. Approaches utilizing bone marrow are considered a promising avenue for regenerative therapy, owing to their potential for transdifferentiation and immunomodulatory characteristics.

Our investigation demonstrated that, in STZ-induced DMT1 mice receiving adoptive transfer of either nBMDC or dBMDC, expression levels of various immune cell types increased notably. These included CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, NK cells, granulocytic neutrophil CD11b+Ly-6G+ myeloid cells, monocytic macrophage CD11b+/Ly-6G− cells, and CD11b+/Ly-6 g− monocytes. Additionally, we observed a significant decrease in the proportion of CD25 + T cells, Foxp3+ cells, Treg CD25/+Foxp3+ cells, Treg CD25+/Foxp3− cells, Treg CD4+/CD25+ cells, and Treg CD4+/CD25− cells within the myeloid cell population in the spleen of STZ-induced DMT1 mice. These findings are consistent with those of Black and Zorina, who indicated that mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are fundamental cellular components of hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) niches in bone marrow (BM) and contribute significantly to hematopoiesis and immunomodulation. MSCs have strong immunoregulatory capacity and can inhibit the proliferation and activity of T lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, Treg CD25+/Foxp3+ cells, Treg CD25+/Foxp3− cells, Treg CD4+/CD25+ cells, and Treg CD4+/CD25− cells, and NK cells. This alleviates autoimmunity and facilitates the regeneration of β cells, restoring euglycemia in T1DM. MSCs also possess the ability to influence T cell responses and create an immunosuppressive local environment, making them promising candidates for therapeutic interventions in various immunological disorders. MSCs have remarkable characteristics, including the ability to evade immune recognition and suppress immune responses.

The results of this study align with the research of Black and Zorina, which identified bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BM-MSCs) as the primary cellular component of bone marrow-derived hematopoietic stem cells (BM-HSCs). BM-MSCs have demonstrated the capacity to enhance autoimmunity in DMT1 by promoting β-cell regeneration and suppressing the activity and proliferation of NK cells, B cells, Tregs, and T cells. Moreover, bone marrow-derived stromal cells (BM-SCs) play a crucial role in promoting angiogenesis by releasing cytokines. BM-SCs also play an important role in immunomodulation by migrating to inflamed areas and altering the phenotype of dendritic cells (DCs), T cells, NK cells, and B cells. BM-MSCs can downregulate pro-inflammatory cytokines, avoid apoptosis mediated by CD8+ T cells, inhibit the proliferation and maturation of DCs, and decrease T-lymphocyte proliferation. Additionally, Weiss and Dahlke indicated that BM-MSCs can inhibit T cell proliferation, including both CD4+ and CD8+ subsets, in a dose-dependent manner during mixed lymphocyte reactions. When interacting with DCs, BM-MSCs facilitate the transition from a pro-inflammatory Th1 cell to an anti-inflammatory Th2 cell, which modifies the cytokine profile toward an anti-inflammatory environment. Furthermore, MSCs exhibit significant inhibitory effects on NK cell proliferation, resulting in diminished cytokine production and cytotoxic activity when co-cultured with these cells.

Administering a single dose of BM-MSCs to prevent the onset of type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) β-cell autoimmunity has been observed to have therapeutic benefits. This clinical effectiveness is associated with the suppressive effects of mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) on allogeneic and autoimmune responses in laboratory settings, as well as the induction of regulatory T cells (Tregs) in laboratory and in vivo experiments. MSCs can also postpone or potentially reverse diabetes progression in non-obese diabetic (NOD) mice by modulating autoimmune responses against islets and suppressing pathogenic CD8+T cells, Th1 cells, and Th17 cells. MSCs can promote Tregs, Treg CD25+/Foxp3+ cells, Treg CD25+/Foxp3−, Treg CD4+/CD25+ cells, and Treg CD4+/CD25− cells through paracrine effects, direct cell receptor interactions, or mitochondrial transfer. Because islets are small, highly vascularized organs, inducing angiogenesis by MSCs within islets is a promising therapeutic approach for T1DM.

Bone marrow cells, MSCs, promote beta-cell regeneration in diabetes. They do so by migrating to the pancreas, enhancing the proliferation of resident progenitor cells, safeguarding existing beta-cells from damage by modulating autophagy, and potentially transdifferentiating into insulin-producing cells. All these actions occur while diminishing harmful inflammation, thus fostering a more favorable environment for the formation and function of new beta-cells.

Altered CD4+/CD8 + T cell ratios are associated with functional outcomes in DMT1, which illustrates the complex nature of the autoimmune response. These imbalances exhibit patterns connected to disease progression, severity, and the potential for gradual beta-cell function decline. However, specific patterns, such as an increase in CD8 + cells or shifts among subsets, vary and highlight different stages or aspects of the disease. A reduced ratio often indicates greater immune dysfunction, and certain types of CD8 + cells, such as exhausted cells, can sometimes predict slower progression.

In diabetes, insulin loss is caused by β-cell death patterns, primarily apoptosis (programmed) and necrosis (accidental). However, new forms of cell death are emerging, such as necroptosis and ferroptosis. Cell survival is linked to inhibiting these pathways (e.g., via anti-apoptotic proteins like Bcl-xL) and balancing stress responses (e.g., oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum [ER] stress) to maintain insulin production. This is evident in resistant β-cells that dedifferentiate but persist, highlighting the existence of complex survival mechanisms that extend beyond the simple states of life and death.

Bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (BMDCs) have significant immunomodulatory and anti-apoptotic properties through direct cell-to-cell interactions and paracrine signaling. Key mechanisms include promoting Treg proliferation, inducing macrophages to transition from a pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype to an anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype that secretes IL-10, and inhibiting the proliferation, differentiation, and migration of B and T lymphocytes, as well as the cytotoxic activity of NK cells. BMDCs secrete immunosuppressive factors, including indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β), and hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), which foster an anti-inflammatory environment. BMDCs also release extracellular vesicles (EVs) and exosomes that transport microRNAs to enhance the function of Tregs and M2 macrophages. BMDCs realize anti-apoptotic effects by modulating apoptosis pathways (FasL/Fas), suppressing caspases, and stimulating pro-survival pathways in stimulated immune cells.

The STZ-induced DMT1 model has its strengths and limitations when it comes to mimicking human disease progression. It is an efficient and cost-effective method of inducing DMT1 in rodents with a single high dose, resulting in rapid hyperglycemia. Unlike genetic models such as NOD mice, it is versatile and applicable to various rodent strains and genders. High doses result in a quick onset, while multiple low doses can gradually cause β-cell death, aiding in the study of diabetic complications and the testing of therapies. However, the STZ-induced DMT1 model has limitations, including inconsistent induction due to variability in dose, strain, and sex; non-autoimmune pathogenesis, unlike the immune basis of human DMT1; off-target organ toxicity, such as in the kidney and liver; potential for fatal hypoglycemia and mortality; lack of insulin resistance; and difficulty simulating the complexity of human disease, particularly concerning the immune response and chronic complications. This frequently necessitates careful protocol optimization, such as adding insulin replacement to make it more relevant to humans.

BMDC-based therapy renews β-cells by influencing endothelial precursor cells, enhancing microvascular angiogenesis, and delivering growth factors, such as hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), which promote β-cell growth and function. BMDC-based therapy improves islet cell function in DMT1 by secreting cytokines and growth factors, promoting angiogenesis and stem cell proliferation, and reducing autoreactive T cells and inflammation. BMDC progenitors can also differentiate into various lineages, which aids in β-cell protection and regeneration, immune response modulation, and blood sugar level reduction. BMDCs can transdifferentiate into β-cells, thereby enhancing glycemic control and supporting regeneration after STZ damage. Furthermore, a small number of BMDCs may transform into pancreatic β-cells. The reversal of hyperglycemia is primarily due to the proliferation of existing β-cells or the suppression of the immune response. This, in turn, promotes β-cell neogenesis and growth.

Regenerative mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-based therapies, including autologous and allogeneic islet cell transplants, show promise in treating DMT1 due to their regenerative and immunomodulatory properties. However, there is limited evidence on their immunogenicity and safety, which necessitates further evaluation. Autologous transplants prevent surgical diabetes, and allogeneic transplants are the standard for DMT1. Although autologous transplantation has low immunogenicity, it faces the re-autoimmunity challenge, necessitating strategies such as encapsulation or gene editing. Allogeneic transplantation has high immunogenicity and requires lifelong immunosuppression. It is also confronted with alloimmunity (rejection by the host) and potential autoimmunity challenges. Both transplantations are considered safe; however, autologous islet cell transplantation is safer, as it carries no risk of GvHD or the need for immunosuppression. Conversely, allogeneic islet cell transplantation carries long-term risks related to immunosuppression, disease transmission, opportunistic infections, and GVHD. Recent strategies aim to engineer both autologous and allogeneic stem cells to be hypoimmunogenic and immune-evasive in order to avoid systemic immunosuppression.
Conclusion

In conclusion, the administration of adoptive transfers of either nBMDC or dBMDC has demonstrated significant immunomodulatory and anti-apoptotic effects on pancreatic β cells. This has a beneficial influence on pancreatic islets in DMT1 mice and combats DMT1 autoimmunity. Adoptive transfer of nBMDC and dBMDC into STZ-induced DMT1 mice modulates immune cell responses, including those of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, NK cells, granulocytic CD11b+/Ly-6G+ cells, monocytic CD11b+/Ly-6G− cells, CD25+ T cells, Foxp3+ cells, Treg CD25+/Foxp3+ cells, Treg CD25+/Foxp3− cells, and Treg CD4+/CD25+ cells. This creates an immunosuppressive environment that protects islet cells from apoptosis and makes nBMDC and dBMDC promising therapeutic agents for various autoimmune disorders, including DMT1. However, clinical studies are needed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of using adoptive transfer of nBMDC or dBMDC in patients with autoimmune DMT1 before they can be considered as a potential therapy for autoimmune DMT1.
